newsitem.title: UK: Saddam's former oil minister gets dewy eyed over Iraq.
newsitem.headline: Saddam's former oil minister gets dewy eyed over Iraq.

text.p: Issam al-Chalabi gets misty-eyed when he talks about the Iraq that could have been.
But though Chalabi shares the sadness of other Iraqis whose homeland lies in tatters after two devastating wars and six years of international sanctions, his pain perhaps runs deeper.
For it was Chalabi, Iraq's oil minister when Saddam Hussein invaded Kuwait in August 1990, who had built Iraq's oil industry back up after an earlier war with Iran that ended after a decade in 1988.
Then he had to see it fall to pieces again after further war damage and years of inactivity under a United Nations embargo.
"I worked in the Iraqi oil industry for over 20 years. It hurts so badly to see the state of the industry after all the work we put in rebuilding from the Iran-Iraq war," Chalabi said.
At the time of the invasion of Kuwait, Iraq could export three million barrels per day and stood behind only Saudi Arabia amongst the world's leading oil suppliers.
Now Iraq produces a meagre 700,000 bpd and exports only a fraction of that to Jordan and through smuggling.
In London for an oil conference, Chalabi was speaking in a rare interview six years to the day that he was sacked by Saddam Hussein.
The official reason for his dismissal was mishandling of gasoline rationing when Iraq was cut off from world trade in response to its conquest of Kuwait.
Chalabai said there were "obviously many other reasons" for his dismissal but did not elaborate. "Who can ever know why or how ministers are picked or dismissed in Iraq?" he said.

Chalabi was the only Iraqi oil minister who came from the ranks of the industry and is still fondly remembered by many ministers and officials at the Organisation of Petroleum Exporting Countries, of which Iraq is a founder member.
"I worked in every single aspect of the industry beginning as a junior engineer. I moved up the ladder every step of the way."

The OPEC meeting he remembers most vividly was just a month before the Kuwaiti invasion. On Saddam's orders, he tried to convince the 12 other OPEC ministers to set a target price of $22 a barrel -- nearly $10 above the market.
It was Saudi Arabia's Hisham Nazer, whose country was soon to be a Gulf War foe, that peruaded the others to set a target of $21, which still stands today.
"Hisham did his best to convince the others to find a deal to accommodate both sides," Chalabi said.
But the OPEC deal and pledges by Kuwait and other quota cheaters to curb production came too late. A few days later, Saddam moved across the border.
Chalabi said he and the other OPEC ministers "had no idea" Saddam would make good on his threats.
"I was shocked. We had hoped the meeting would have eased the tensions but he (Saddam) had already made up his mind."
He said he and some other cabinet ministers found out about the pre-dawn invasion after it happened. "I knew nothing until I went into my office," he said.
Chalabi now works as an oil consultant in Jordan, a neighbour of Iraq.
"After six years I have decided to speak out now because someone needs to talk about the needless suffering of the Iraqi people. Still I know not to take a political stance," he said.
But the fact that he appeared in public this week questioning whether Baghdad really wanted to sell oil via a stalled U.N. plan to pay for food and medical supplies is remarkable enough.

The deal allowing Iraq to sell $2 billion worth of oil over six months was signed in May but in late August, just weeks away from implementation, Saddam Hussein got involved in Kurdish fighting in Northern Iraq, drawing U.S. military retaliation and put the deal on hold for perhaps months.
"I do not see an end to sanctions under the present (Iraqi) regime and I do not see a quick return of exports under the one- time sale. Both sides put up obstacles," he said.
